data.title: Dem Lawmaker Spots 1 Thing That Makes Her Think Trump Is 'Hitting The Panic Button'
data.description:
Dem Lawmaker Spots 1 Thing That Makes Her Think Trump Is 'Hitting The Panic Button'

Pocharapon Neammanee
Sat, 12 September 2026 at 9:26 pm UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.) says President Donald Trump's bizarre end to his Republican midterm convention on Thursday, where he led the audience in a pledge to him, is a sign of panic.  

"It's definitely a president trying to hit the panic button because he knows his poll numbers are in the tank. He knows that Americans have seen through the act that he put forward," Jayapal said on MS Now's "The Assignment" Saturday. "I mean, this is an incompetent, corrupt cult leader president. He promised a lot of things."

Jayapal's harsh criticism of the president comes days after the unprecedented Republican convention, where he asked his supporters on Thursday to raise their right hands and recite: "I pledge to the greatest president in the history of the United States."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"That I will go out with my family, my friends, I'll do it anyway, I don't care if I'm registered or not. I'm going to try and cheat like hell like they do," he continued. "There's never been bigger cheaters, they don't care. I am going to go out and I am going to get my friends, my family, and we are going to vote on November 3rd or we are going to vote before that."

Like this article? Keep independent journalism alive. Support HuffPost.

The Democratic congresswoman told host Antonia Hylton that it's dangerous "to have a president who is asking people to pledge allegiance to him, supposedly endowed by God to deliver for them when they have seen over and over again that this man is delivering for no one except him and his billionaire cronies and his family."

Politics: For The First Time, House Votes To End Iran War In Rebuke To Trump

The president is facing sinking approval ratings in his second term as Americans feel the impact of his war in Iran. Some of Trump's most vocal supporters during his presidential campaign have split from him over unfulfilled promises. 

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"I think the next Republican nominee is going to have to decide if they are going to continue to pledge loyalty to the cult of Donald Trump, or if they are actually going to represent Republicans across the country who want something very different," Jayapal said. 

She told Hylton "he's hitting the panic button because he knows he's in trouble."

After several unfulfilled promises, Trump now faces skepticism and backlash after he promised every American $5,000 if Republicans winthe midterm elections. Jayapal, however, said, "It has a chance in hell."

"The same thing when he says he's going to end the war and gas prices are going to go plummeting after the midterm elections. I'm sorry, but if he could do that, why wouldn't he have done that now, or three months ago, or six months ago?" she argued.

data.title: Russian attacks kill nine, injure dozens in Ukraine; Russia says it hits ships, plants
data.description:
Russian attacks kill nine, injure dozens in Ukraine; Russia says it hits ships, plants

Reuters
Sat, 12 September 2026 at 8:52 pm UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Russian drone attack in Chornomorsk

1 of 3
Children hold parts of a Russian drone near a hotel damaged during a Russian drone strike, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in the city of Chornomorsk, Odesa region, Ukraine September 12, 2026. REUTERS/Nina Liashonok

KYIV, Sept 12 (Reuters) - Russian air strikes in several Ukrainian regions on Saturday killed nine people, injured dozens and damaged residential buildings and infrastructure across the country, officials said.

The civilian death toll has risen sharply in Ukraine over the past two months as ‌Russia steps up attacks on power plants and other infrastructure. Ukraine has hit energy facilities and warehouses in distant parts of Russia, and ‌both sides have targeted each other's shipping.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, writing on Telegram, said Russia had deployed nearly 500 drones against Ukrainian targets since early morning.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"Basically, the Russians have expanded the ​war away from the front, where they have no success, into the economy, and their tactics are as basic as it gets: destroying every site that could help people cope with the conditions of war," Zelenskiy wrote.

"Russia wants to kill the Ukrainian economy and break our resistance," Zelenskiy added.

The city council in Kramatorsk, one of Ukraine's frontline "fortress cities" that Russia wants to capture, said Russian forces attacked private cars, killing three people in three incidents over a 90-minute period. Four people were ‌injured.

"These are not military targets," the council said. "They are ⁠ordinary civilian cars. People were going about their business."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The governor of Ukraine's Zhytomyr Region, west of Kyiv, Vitaliy Bunechko, said a Russian strike on a grocery store killed two people in the town of Zvyahel. Bunechko said two petrol stations ⁠also came under attack as well as an unidentified "enterprise with foreign investment."

Earlier, Zelenskiy reported attacks on the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia and Kryvyi Rih, his hometown.

The governor of Zaporizhzhia Region, Ivan Fedorov, said two people were killed and 11 injured in assaults on Zaporizhzhia and other localities.

Oleksandr Vilkul, head of Kryvyi Rih's military administration, said two people ​were ​killed in overnight attacks on the city by drones and missiles.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The Russian military said its ​forces hit Ukrainian steel maker Zaporizhstal in the city of ‌Zaporizhzhia, an Interpipe Steel complex in Dnipro and several plants in Kryvyi Rih, including the Northern Iron Ore Beneficiation Works complex.

Reuters could not independently verify accounts from either side.

In Odesa Region, Governor Oleh Kiper said 37 people, including an infant, were injured in a series of overnight attacks. Two people were missing.

In Moldova, on Ukraine's western border, authorities closed national airspace for nearly an hour after a drone was detected near the border. Seven border crossings were temporarily closed.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Russian drones have regularly entered Moldovan airspace despite official protests. During one instance this week, the departure of Zelenskiy's aircraft to Norway was delayed.

RUSSIAN STRIKES ON UKRAINIAN ‌PORT

The Russian Defence Ministry said Russia's forces have maintained their strikes on Ukrainian ports, ​hitting a cargo ship in Odesa it said was carrying goods for military use.

Earlier in the ​day, the ministry said its forces struck two cargo vessels overnight ​in the port of Chornomorsk.

Ukraine's military said it hit one of Russia's largest synthetic rubber producers in Togliatti in the ‌Samara region, causing a fire. The Togliattikauchuk plant specialised in the ​production of synthetic rubbers and fuel additives ​that are used in fuel for Russian missiles, it said.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Russian regional governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said industrial facilities in Samara region had been attacked by Ukrainian drones, without specifying which they were or whether they had been damaged, Interfax news agency reported.

Ilya Sukhikh, mayor of the city of ​Togliatti in Samara region, said several residential buildings were ‌damaged and one person was injured.

In a separate attack, four commercial properties were set ablaze in the city of Taganrog in ​the Rostov region, local mayor Svetlana Kambulova said, according to TASS.

(Reporting by Olena Harmash and Maxim Rodionov and Alexander Tanas in Chisinau; ​Editing by Peter Graff, Ron Popeski, Will Dunham, Philippa Fletcher and Chizu Nomiyama)

data.title: Yemen government forces say hit Houthis in Red Sea city
data.description:
Yemen government forces say hit Houthis in Red Sea city

AFP News
Sat, 12 September 2026 at 7:54 pm UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Yemen's Saudi-backed government forces said Saturday that they had struck Iran-allied Houthi fighters in the Red Sea city of Mocha, as the number of civilians forced to flee the renewed fighting soared.

US news site Axios reported that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman had twice called US President Donald Trump to request American strikes on the Houthis last week but the request was rejected.

The ongoing clashes follow a week-long Houthi offensive that culminated in the group capturing the remainder of Yemen's Red Sea coast and several strategic islands, and cementing their hold on the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the sea's southern entrance.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The waterway has become an important artery for Saudi Arabian oil exports after Iran largely cut off shipments through the Gulf with its blockade on the Strait of Hormuz at the start of the Middle East war. The Houthis have recently declared their own maritime blockade of Riyadh's Red Sea ports.

The government news agency Saba reported on Saturday that Yemeni "forces destroyed vehicles and weapons and killed members of the Houthi terrorist militia" near the port of Mocha, and quoted a spokesman for the forces as saying they had also struck Houthi targets just outside the city.

The Houthis, meanwhile, said on Saturday evening that over the past 48 hours, "Saudi enemy aircraft conducted 129 airstrikes" on areas under their control.

Yemen's civil war, which began in 2014 with the Houthi capture of the capital Sanaa, had been dormant since a ceasefire in 2022 but roared back to life in July.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Saudi Arabia first entered the war on the side of Yemen's internationally recognised government in 2015 and continues to support the Aden-based administration.

On Saturday night, Saudi authorities said a Houthi projectile fell in an area near the border, hours after issuing alerts warning of the risk of possible attacks.

The civil defence directorate said the incident resulted "in two injuries and material damage to a mosque, several buildings, and vehicles".

- 'Not even a shelter' -

The Yemeni civil war uprooted millions of people, and the latest fighting has led even more to flee their homes.

The fall of Mocha to the Houthis on Thursday drove many residents to Aden, where the internationally recognised government is based.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

One of the displaced, Abdulali al-Rajihi, said the Houthis "told us: 'Leave, scatter, you have half an hour'".

"We fled wearing the clothes on our backs. And we took our children, as much as we could manage."

Saddam Ali escaped from Al-Waziyah with his 11 children and a few possessions crammed into a small pick-up truck. He said he hadn't found a single free house in the city, "not even a shelter".

The UN's migration agency said on Saturday that, since July, 76,000 people had fled the fighting, a figure that had quadrupled since last week.

It said it was providing support but warned that "needs are far outpacing what we can deliver".

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"The situation is deteriorating by the day," it added.

The renewed fighting in Yemen has killed more than 500 people, according to sources on both sides.

- 'Fine and dandy' -

Following the Axios report on the Saudi request for help, Trump on Saturday acknowledged speaking to the de facto Saudi leader, but said the Houthis had also "called us and they don't want to fight with us".

He did not elaborate on whether the United States would take any action, but he told reporters that "everything's gonna work out fine and dandy" in the region.

In 2025, the United States conducted a seven-week bombing campaign against the Houthis in response to their repeated attacks on Red Sea shipping in support of Hamas in the Gaza war.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

That effort ended with a negotiated ceasefire, though the Houthis kept up their missile and drone attacks targeting Israel.

More recently, the group has resumed attacks on ships in the Red Sea after declaring their maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia.

In the capital Sanaa, meanwhile, Houthi supporters were celebrating the freeing of 210 prisoners held in areas that fell to the group.

The group said they were prisoners of war who had spent up to eight years in jail.

"I have rediscovered the taste of life," freed prisoner Mohammed Bajash told AFP. "For five years, I suffered every day."

data.title: Trump Tells Smithsonian Institution To Install George Washington Statues And Exhibit
data.description:
Trump Tells Smithsonian Institution To Install George Washington Statues And Exhibit

Jamie Ding / AP
Sat, 12 September 2026 at 8:55 pm UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

President Donald Trump wants the Smithsonian Institution to install a colossal statue of George Washington outside the National Museum of American History and a special exhibit honoring the nation's first president.

Politics: Trump Floods Truth Social With Bizarre Posts On 9/11 Anniversary

Trump, in social media posts late Friday, asked for an exhibit beginning now and continuing through Feb. 22, 2032, the 300th anniversary of Washington's birth. For Constitution Day on Sept. 17, Trump asked the institution to install the 11-foot statue of Washington featured at the recent Freedom 250 IndyCar race in the museum's Flag Hall.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

He also wants a 30-foot statue of Washington to replace the current "Infinity" sculpture by New York artist Jose de Rivera, commissioned by the federal government and installed in 1967.

Like this article? Keep independent journalism alive. Support HuffPost.

"He is easily America's Greatest Hero. Without him, our Country and our Freedoms wouldn't exist," Trump posted on Truth Social as he flew to his golf course in Ireland.

He complained that the museum currently doesn't mention Washington's fabled crossing of the Delaware River during the Revolutionary War.

Politics: Trump Visits Ireland, Putin Warns Europe Against Sending Troops To Ukraine: Live Updates

Instead of a Center for Restorative History — a recently ended museum initiative to spotlight spotlights stories that have been excluded from the national historical narrative — Trump said the museum should have a "Center for American Heroes."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

It's not clear that Trump has the power to order the museum to make the change. The Smithsonian operates outside the executive branch and its leadership is overseen by a Board of Regents that includes Vice President JD Vance, Chief Justice John Roberts, a bipartisan group of lawmakers and a group of citizens.

Trump in March revealed his intention to force changes at the Smithsonian with an executive order that targeted funding for programs that advanced "divisive narratives" and "improper ideology."

The White House published a lengthy report this year that repeatedly complained the institution had not done enough to highlight Washington and other founders.

Politics: Congress Is Starting To Argue About A Potential AI Apocalypse

In July, he ordered his administration to install signs in front of the U.S. history museum telling visitors that some of the exhibits are inaccurate, part of his initiatives to reshape how the story of the United States is told.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Its top leader, Lonnie Bunch, announced this week he was stepping down at the end of the year.

Statues have also been a consistent theme in Trump's many efforts to remake Washington. He wants to build a park along the Potomac River to display statues of 250 prominent Americans, and he has also installed a statue of Washington in his remodeled Rose Garden patio.

data.title: Trump says Irish unification would be ‘fantastic,’ wading into sensitive topic during weekend visit
data.description:
Trump says Irish unification would be ‘fantastic,’ wading into sensitive topic during weekend visit

Kit Maher, Issy Ronald, Niamh Kennedy, CNN
Sat, 12 September 2026 at 8:49 pm UTC
7 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

President Donald Trump said Saturday that Irish reunification "would be a fantastic thing" during a bilateral meeting with Ireland's taoiseach, Micheál Martin, something he projected is "going to happen eventually."

When a reporter asked his view on the topic, Trump at first acknowledged his comments could inflame a politically sensitive issue before voicing support.

"Well, I don't want to cause any trouble," Trump said Saturday. "But I will tell you, I'd love to see it unified."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The reunification of Ireland has long been considered a contentious issue, dividing opinion among the unionists, typically from Protestant backgrounds, who would like Northern Ireland to remain part of the United Kingdom and nationalists, typically from Catholic backgrounds, who would like to see it reunited with the Republic of Ireland.

For nearly 30 years, Northern Ireland was plagued by significant sectarian violence and disorder, in a period known as the Troubles. Under the US-brokered 1998 "Good Friday" agreement, which largely ended the conflict, a majority of voters in border polls held both in the north and south would need to be in favor of reunification for this to take place. Wary of such sensitivities, US presidents have typically avoided explicitly commenting on the issue, even President Joe Biden, who frequently referenced his Irish heritage.

Trump's comments were almost immediately met with pushback from the UK government and unionists. Downing Street pointed CNN to newly installed Prime Minister Andy Burnham's comments in August when he downplayed the prospect of an imminent border poll in Northern Ireland. That is "off the table," he said, later confirming he would "100%" follow the Good Friday Agreement.

Gavin Robinson, who leads the Democratic Unionist Party, said that Northern Ireland's future "will be decided by the people of Northern Ireland, not by commentary in London, Dublin or Washington."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

However, Trump seemed confident the move would happen eventually and questioned how it could be a negative thing.

"It's going to happen eventually. … I think it will happen now. You've got the right man over here to get it moving," Trump said, pointing at Martin. "But yeah, I think it would be a fantastic thing. Now the UK will have something to say about obviously, but I think it would be a great thing."

Trump touched down in Ireland on Saturday morning to hold talks with the country's leaders before attending a tournament at one of his golf courses.

Trump's son Donald Trump Jr. and his wife, Bettina, disembarked from the plane afterward and also greeted officials on the ground.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

During the visit, President Trump heard an Irish band play the American national anthem, immediately followed by the Irish anthem, while Irish President Catherine Connolly stood by. Trump briefly answered a couple of questions after the courtesy call with Connolly, including one concerning traffic through the Bab al-Mandeb strait.

"Everything will work out just fine. It's all going to work out fine," Trump said.

This visit takes Trump out the US at a crucial time for him politically, just weeks before the midterms and as the Iran-backed Houthis' rapid advance in Yemen threatens to open a second front in the war with Tehran.

During his time in Ireland, Trump will largely be shielded from the public and kept away from expected protests. Instead, he was ferried by motorcade straight to three official government residences in Phoenix Park, a huge urban park in central Dublin, which officials have closed since Friday night.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

There, he held a bilateral meeting with the taoiseach and delivered remarks to business leaders at US Ambassador to Ireland Edward Walsh's residence.

The president's meetings with Irish political leaders will touch on bilateral economic cooperation, creating business opportunities for US industry, and discussing international issues of mutual interest, a White House official told CNN.

Protests of Trump's visit

Trump's visit presents a tricky balancing act for the Irish government. On the one hand, US companies, many of whom have their European headquarters in Ireland, are hugely important for the country's economy. On the other, Trump remains unpopular with much of the Irish public.

Thousands of people joined an anti-Trump march through central Dublin on Saturday afternoon, several of them waving Palestinian flags.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"We don't want him here," Eudie Moriarty from County Clare told CNN. "We respect the president of America always. But not this president."

Protests also took place in Doonbeg, the village in the west of Ireland where Trump's golf course is located, and at Shannon Airport.

Anti-war activist groups have held demonstrations at the airport over the years protesting the US military's use of the facility as a refueling stop for its troops, and then-President Ronald Reagan's visit to Ireland in 1984 was also marked by protests.

Asked about the planned protests against his visit in Ireland, Trump said he was unaware of them.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"I didn't know there was a protest," Trump said. "It can't be a very big one, because we've been all over Ireland today already," though he had just landed in Dublin a couple of hours prior.

CNN photojournalist William Bonnett captured a small group of about 20 to 30 protesters in Doonbeg and Shannon on Saturday morning. One woman held a sign that read, "We do not like you here nor there. We do not like you ANYWHERE!"

After wrapping up his meetings in Dublin, Trump traveled west on Saturday to his Doonbeg course, where he attended the Irish Open tournament.

His son Eric Trump told Irish national broadcaster RTÉ that the golf course is the largest employer in the local area.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"Go down to Morrissey's tavern in Doonbeg and hear from a real Irish person as to whether or not they like President Trump and the Trump family," he said. "Go have them attest to what we've done for the country and what we've invested in the country and the love and respect that our family has always shown them."

Connolly was among those who protested Trump's visit in 2019 before she was elected to the ceremonial position of Ireland's president in 2025. She was extremely critical of Trump during that campaign, describing him as "somebody who armed and funded genocide." For his part, Trump referred to Connolly as a "he" in March when asked by an Irish reporter about her comments about "violations of international law" in the Middle East.

"Look, he's lucky I exist, that's all I can say," Trump said. "If you're gonna allow countries that are sick and demented — and they are demented — to have nuclear weapons, everybody in the whole world should be very thankful."

If there was any tension between Connolly and Trump, he didn't hint at it, calling her "terrific" during his remarks at the embassy later. In a statement released by her office, Connolly took a slightly more forceful course, saying she "conveyed the strong view of the Irish people that the normalization of war and genocide can never be accepted."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

While Trump said he hates "what's happening with Europe" on immigration and trade, he gave effusive praise to the people of Ireland, one of two European Union countries where English is listed as one of the official languages, with somewhat of a backhanded compliment about their toughness.

"People love coming to Ireland. You know why? Because they love you. They love the people. There's a friendliness. There's, uh, there's also a vicious and a toughness," Trump said. "Let me tell you, you are some of the most vicious bastards I've ever (seen). But when you want to be nice, there's nobody nicer."

This story has been updated with additional developments.

CORRECTION: This story has been updated to reflect that English is the official language in two European Union countries. It was also updated with the correct 1998 signing date of the Good Friday Agreement.

data.title: New video shows interaction between NYC Mayor Mamdani and AOC at 9/11 ceremony after the moment sparked debate
data.description:
New video shows interaction between NYC Mayor Mamdani and AOC at 9/11 ceremony after the moment sparked debate

Emma Tucker, CNN
Sat, 12 September 2026 at 8:41 pm UTC
5 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

A brief interaction between New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez captured on video Friday during a ceremony marking the 25th anniversary of the terror attacks on September 11, 2001, sparked fierce criticism that was met with pushback from those who say the video was taken out of context.

The clip of Mamdani and Ocasio-Cortez at Ground Zero lasted four seconds in Friday's live video feed, which transitioned between multiple camera angles of the ceremony.

In the pool footage of an isolated camera, viewed by CNN, a longer clip shows Mamdani standing with a solemn expression as the names of the attack victims are called before briefly greeting the congresswoman.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Ocasio-Cortez steps up beside the mayor, places her hand on his elbow and they exchange smiles and a brief embrace, the video shows. They then exchange words and Mamdani hugs her briefly. The mayor, smiling, says something to Ocasio-Cortez, who smiles broadly. They then stand side by side as the reading of the names continues, applauding after a statement by the daughter of a police officer who died on 9/11.

CNN has reached out to representatives for Mamdani and Ocasio-Cortez for comment.

Their exchange has prompted debate around the moment, with some Republicans criticizing the two New York Democrats for what they called inappropriate laughter and others saying that characterization is false.

The former head of security for Rudy Giuliani – who was the city's mayor during the terror attacks – said videos of the two leaders "laughing are not true."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Michael Ragusa wrote on social media he was standing next to Mamdani and Ocasio-Cortez for the entire ceremony.

"The camera just caught her greeting him hello. Multiple other politicians were laughing and joking behind me. Republicans and Democrats," Ragusa said on X.

Texas Sen. Ted Cruz reposted the video clip on X, saying, "How the hell do you laugh while the names of those murdered on 9/11 are being read aloud?"

Another attendee, former Democratic New York State Assemblymember Yuh-Line Niou, condemned the criticism as "ridiculous talking points."

She noted most politicians don't stay for the duration of the ceremony, but Mamdani "stayed for every name and even stayed after to talk to families for 45 minutes."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Ocasio-Cortez also stayed until the end, Niou wrote on X, adding the brief interaction with Mamdani "was just when she walked up to him and said hello."

Another criticism came from Meghan McCain, conservative television personality and daughter of the late Republican Sen. John McCain. "Why the f**k are these two laughing?!?" she wrote on X.

Niou, however, said she has attended the Ground Zero ceremony every year for the past decade, adding: "My friends and neighbors are not crying for 6 hours straight."

"We are greeting each other, hugging each other, laughing at the memories and the jokes the families tell remembering their loved ones," Niou said.

In the moments before the ceremony began, Mamdani, the city's first Muslim mayor, walked over to Giuliani to shake his hand at the Ground Zero ceremony.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The brief moment was also caught by cameras and reaction was swift on social media, with some praising Mamdani for showing grace to the man who just a few days prior had compared him to 9/11 hijackers and said his presence at the memorial ceremony would be offensive.

Aides to the mayor said Mamdani and Giuliani "exchanged pleasantries," and that Giuliani told Mamdani that the job of being mayor was hard.

Friday's exchange appeared to offer a brief pause on the political rancor of the past weeks.

An aide to Giuliani said the former mayor told Mamdani he was "praying for him."

Speaking briefly with reporters after the event, Mamdani declined to share what the former mayor had said to him.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"He came over and we both extended our hands and exchanged pleasantries," Mamdani said, according to remarks shared by his office.

"I think the focus for all of us is a focus on the families, a focus on first responders and to be here and hear the names of all those who were stolen from us 25 years ago and how the families have persevered through that time. I am truly in awe of all that these families have given us."

Mamdani has faced partisan rancor around his attendance at the ceremony for weeks.

Giuliani previously said Mamdani attending the commemoration "offends" him, while George Pataki, state governor during the disaster, said Mamdani should stay away. Bruce Blakeman, a candidate for governor, had vowed to turn his back on the mayor if he turns up.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Later in the day after attending the ceremony, Mamdani spoke at an interfaith memorial service at St. Nicholas Greek Orthodox Church and National Shrine, the only house of worship that was destroyed on 9/11.

Mamdani recalled the resiliency of New Yorkers in the aftermath of the tragedy as he spoke. "Those who attacked our city, they did so because they thought they could break us at the fractures," he said.

"They thought they could frighten us. They could make us feel alone. They could leave us on our knees," Mamdani said. "How wrong they were. How quick we were to stand back up."

CNN's Gloria Pazmino and Elise Hammond contributed to this report.

For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com

data.title: Trump says Irish unification would be 'fantastic'
data.description:
Trump says Irish unification would be 'fantastic'

Brendan Smialowski, with Peter Hutchison and Aurelia End in Dublin
Sat, 12 September 2026 at 8:47 pm UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Donald Trump said Saturday he would "love to see" a united Ireland, wading into a politically sensitive subject as he embarked on a two-day Irish visit that blurs the lines between his presidency and personal business interests.

After meeting Ireland's Prime Minister Micheal Martin in Dublin, Trump said reunification of the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland -- split for over a century -- would be "a fantastic thing".

"It's going to happen eventually. It may as well happen now," he told reporters, adding "the UK will have something to say about it, obviously".

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The island of Ireland has been split between the Irish republic in the south and Northern Ireland, which is part of the United Kingdom, since 1921.

Under the 1998 Good Friday Agreement, which ended three decades of sectarian violence in Northern Ireland that killed about 3,000 people, a referendum can be held if the UK government determines a majority there is likely to favour joining the Republic of Ireland.

Republic of Ireland voters would also have to endorse reunification in a poll for it to happen.

The United States has previously adopted a neutral position on the issue.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham insisted last month that a unity referendum was "off the table", drawing a sharp response from the pro-unity party Sinn Fein.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Asked about Trump's comments, a spokesperson for his Downing Street office referred reporters to comments Burnham made in parliament Wednesday when he vowed to "stick to the Good Friday Agreement 100 percent".

However Gavin Robinson, leader of the pro-British Democratic Unionist Party, said on X that "as unionists we are not interested in the destruction of our country by joining with the Irish Republic".

- Divergences -

Trump had touched down at Dublin airport shortly before 8:25 am (0725 GMT) under a security operation dubbed one of the largest ever mounted in Ireland and reportedly costing 20 million euros ($23 million).

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

At least 4,000 police and other personnel, including snipers, have been mobilised.

In Dublin, at least 2,000 protesters waving Palestinian flags and holding placards rallied Saturday lunchtime against the president's visit, chanting "Donald Trump's not welcome here", AFP reporters saw.

One sign read "no imperialists in Ireland" while some held explicit inflatable balloons showing Trump in sex acts with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

"Trump is a warmonger," student Cillian Whelan, 19, told AFP. "He has no right to be in my country. He should be on trial."

One small group of demonstrators -- dressed in black and wearing masks and dark glasses -- set a US flag on fire, according to The Irish Times.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Smaller protests also occurred at Shannon Airport, where the US leader transited, and in Doonbeg on Ireland's west coast, where the Trump Organization's 2014-purchased course is hosting golf's Irish Open tournament.

Police said three women -- aged in their 20s, 30s and 40s -- had appeared in a western Irish court late Saturday after being arrested for separate trespass and public order offences there.

After completing engagements in Dublin, Trump made a dramatic landing in Doonbeg aboard Marine One, and was soon photographed watching over the 18th green during the third round of the Open flanked by his sons Don Jr. and Eric.

He was reportedly given a rapturous reception during a brief appearance in the resort's members' bar, with drinkers chanting "USA".

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

- 'Strong view' -

Earlier in Dublin, Trump appeared to receive a frostier reception from left-wing President Catherine Connolly, an outspoken critic of the US leader.

"I conveyed the strong view of the Irish people that the normalisation of war and genocide can never be accepted," Connolly said in a post-meeting statement.

He then met Martin, when the Iran war and US tariffs on EU pharmaceuticals and immigration were on the agenda.

Ireland and the United States have long been close allies, partly because of their common ancestral ties.

But the Irish government's politics diverge sharply from those of the Trump administration on many issues, with Ireland being one of Europe's most pro-Palestinian countries.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

It is among several countries, including Spain, the UK and France, that have announced a trade ban targeting Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

In Doonbeg, some 40,000 fans are expected at the Open over the weekend. Trump may even award the trophy Sunday.

The 80-year-old golf-mad president has promoted his family's courses and other businesses unabashedly since returning to the White House for his second presidential stint in January 2025.

Trinity College Dublin US history professor Daniel Gear told AFP that Trump "sees little difference between his private interests and his role as president".

data.title: Kyiv preparing for talks to resume in October, senior Ukrainian official says
data.description:
Kyiv preparing for talks to resume in October, senior Ukrainian official says

Reuters
Sat, 12 September 2026 at 7:44 pm UTC
1 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Ukraine's President Zelenskiy welcomes U.S. special representatives Witkoff and Kushner in Kyiv

1 of 2
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskiy meets with Jared Kushner, U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law, and U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in Kyiv, Ukraine September 6, 2026. Ukrainian Presidential Press Service/Handout via REUTERS

Sept 12 (Reuters) - Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy's chief of staff was quoted as saying on Saturday that Kyiv was preparing ‌for the resumption in October of three-sided talks aimed ‌at resolving the more than 4-1/2-year-old war with Russia.

Kyrylo Budanov, quoted by Ukrainian media, ​told reporters on the sidelines of a conference in Kyiv that Ukraine was readying itself for the prospect of new talks involving Russia and the United States.

"We are getting ready. In October," Budanov was quoted as ‌saying.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Budanov was speaking several ⁠days after U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held talks in both Moscow and Kyiv. It was ⁠their first such visit to Moscow since February and their first visit to the Ukrainian capital.

The last three-sided meeting took place in Geneva ​in February. ​U.S.-led diplomatic efforts had stalled as ​Washington was focused on the ‌conflict with Iran.

Witkoff said after visiting both capitals that they welcomed new momentum in proceeding with talks.

Zelenskiy said the two envoys had presented some "very decent, worthwhile ideas". He suggested that a new three-sided meeting could be hosted by Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, Switzerland or ‌other countries.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Moscow ​did not rule out a resumption ​of peace talks but added ​that it was too early to say when ‌and where such talks might take ​place.

Major differences on ​how to end the war remain between the two sides. A key issue is the fate of the remaining Ukrainian-held territory ​in the eastern Donbas ‌region, which Moscow has claimed as its own but has ​failed to capture despite years of fierce fighting.

data.title: Trump Trashes NATO Over Refusal To Join Iran War: 'Why The Hell Are We Helping Them?'
data.description:
Trump Trashes NATO Over Refusal To Join Iran War: 'Why The Hell Are We Helping Them?'

Marco Margaritoff
Sat, 12 September 2026 at 7:43 pm UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

President Donald Trump criticized NATO on Saturday over its continued refusal to participate in the ongoing U.S. war on Iran and "help" the U.S. with Iran's dynamic control of the Strait of Hormuz.

NATO has been a frequent target for Trump, who reiterated his complaints during a speech at the Deerfield Residence in Dublin, the official home of the U.S. ambassador to Ireland, after stating, "I sort of hate to see what's happening with Europe."

Politics: Trump Visits Ireland, Putin Warns Europe Against Sending Troops To Ukraine: Live Updates

"I hate to see what's happening on trade, I hate to see what's happening on energy, and I hate to see what's happening on immigration," said Trump. "Woo, that immigration. What you're doing to yourselves, you're just killing yourselves. But we're going to work with them."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

He added, "Very disappointing in many ways, that NATO didn't want to help us with the strait, even though we don't get any oil from the strait. We don't need it. We have a lot of oil. We have more oil than anybody, as you know, but we thought it was important."

A fifth of the world's oil passes through the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran has essentially tightened its grip on since the start of the war. This has driven oil prices up: It is trading at more than $100 per barrel for the first time in months. 

Trump has offered muddy reasoning for launching the war and hasn't reached any of the stated objectives he laid out earlier this year. He has consistently expressed his frustration with NATO allies.

"I said, 'Would you like to help us with the Hormuz strait?'" Trump said regarding NATO on Saturday. He recalled European leaders turning him down, before appearing to suggest that he declined their support himself: "But I put it down because, why the hell are we helping them? So, you'll be hearing that later." 

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Like this article? Keep independent journalism alive. Support HuffPost.

Trump has caused notable friction with French President Emmanuel Macron, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, and other NATO leaders for failing to consult them before his war — which has disrupted the world economy and sparked fears of a global energy crisis.

Trump, who is visiting Ireland for the closing weekend of the 2026 Amgen Irish Open at his Doonbeg golf resort, even claimed NATO is "saving us a lot of money" by opting out of his war, stating, "I didn't do a heavy sell. I didn't do a Trump kind of a sell."
